short: South Africa has no AI law or adopted AI policy: the Cabinet-approved Draft National AI Policy of 10 April 2026 was withdrawn in its entirety on 12 June 2026. POPIA binds, including its rule on decisions based solely on automated processing.
title: South Africa AI Laws
subtitle: No AI law: a draft AI policy withdrawn, and POPIA on automated decisions
body_html:
Status at a glance

No AI law or adopted AI policy. The Department of Communications and Digital Technologies published a Cabinet-approved Draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy for comment on 10 April 2026 (General Notice 3880 of 2026). On 12 June 2026 it was withdrawn in its entirety (General Notice 3978 of 2026), and Cabinet approved the withdrawal. South Africa therefore has no AI law and no adopted AI policy. The binding layer is the Protection of Personal Information Act, whose section 71 restricts decisions based solely on automated processing. Verified on 25 October 2026 against the Government Gazette on gov.za and SAnews.

Key instruments

InstrumentNumberDateStatus
Draft South Africa National Artificial Intelligence PolicyGeneral Notice 3880 of 2026, Government Gazette 54477Published 10 April 2026, after Cabinet approvalWithdrawn by General Notice 3978 of 2026, Gazette 54840, 12 June 2026
Protection of Personal Information Act, 2013Act No. 4 of 2013; Gazette 37067Assented to 19 November 2013; published 26 November 2013In force

Who regulates and enforces

  • Information Regulator: enforces POPIA, including section 71.
  • Department of Communications and Digital Technologies: owns AI policy.

Scope and reach

POPIA applies to responsible parties domiciled in South Africa, and to those not domiciled there that use automated or non-automated means in South Africa, unless the means are used only to forward information through the country (s. 3(1)(b)).

Core obligations

  • A data subject may not be subject to a decision with legal consequences or a substantial effect that is based solely on automated processing intended to profile them, except as section 71(2) allows (POPIA s. 71(1)).
  • The rest of POPIA's conditions for lawful processing.

Penalties

BreachMaximumProvisionEnforcer
An offence dealt with by infringement noticeAn administrative fine of up to R10 millionPOPIA s. 109(2)(c)Information Regulator
Offences under ss. 100, 103(1), 104(2), 105(1) and 106(1), (3) and (4)A fine, imprisonment of up to 10 years, or bothPOPIA s. 107(a)Courts

What is coming next

  • A reworked AI policy; Cabinet said the policy would be revised, and no official date has been published.

Why the policy was withdrawn, and what replaces it

Cabinet approved the draft on 25 March 2026, with a special sitting on 1 April; the Gazette notice of 10 April 2026 gave the public until 10 June 2026 to comment. On 26 April 2026 Minister Solly Malatsi announced its withdrawal after a News24 report found that roughly a tenth of the draft's academic references did not exist and appeared to have been generated by an AI tool; two departmental officials were placed on precautionary suspension. The formal withdrawal notice is dated 4 June 2026 and was gazetted on 12 June. The department briefed Parliament's portfolio committee on 26 May 2026, said it still aimed to finalise a revised policy in the 2026/27 financial year, and appointed an independent panel of AI researchers, lawyers and governance specialists, reported to be chaired by Professor Benjamin Rosman, to rebuild the text on verifiable evidence before it is republished; no date for the new draft has been given. The withdrawn draft had proposed seven new bodies, among them a National AI Commission, an AI Ethics Board, an AI Insurance Superfund and a National AI Safety Institute, and critics in TechCentral and elsewhere argued the revised version should instead strengthen the mandates of regulators that already exist: ICASA, the Information Regulator, the Competition Commission and the National Consumer Commission.

The withdrawn draft was built on the South Africa National AI Policy Framework of August 2024, which drew 32 public submissions, so the direction of travel is known even though the text is not: a national framework giving effect to POPIA, the Promotion of Access to Information Act and the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act rather than a standalone AI statute. DLA Piper and Mondaq commentators expect the fundamental approach to survive the rewrite.

Until a policy is adopted, POPIA is the whole of the binding law. Section 71 bars decisions based solely on automated processing that have legal or similarly significant effects, unless a lawful exception applies; the purpose-limitation condition in section 13 stops personal information collected for one purpose being reused to train a model without a lawful basis; and the Information Regulator, an independent body under Chapter 5 of the Act, enforces through information notices, assessments and enforcement notices, with sectoral codes of conduct possible under section 61. The Regulator's regulations of 17 April 2025 (GN 6126) are the latest procedural layer. A company deploying AI in South Africa should document its section 71 position now; that duty will not change whatever the revised policy says.

Last verified

4 November 2026, against the sources above. The reasons for the withdrawal, the suspensions, the expert panel and the 2026/27 target are as the South African press reports the department's statements to Parliament, not read on dcdt.gov.za, which was under maintenance. Not confirmed on an official source and therefore left out: the text of the 2024 National AI Policy Framework.
